q-177651:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}=[-0.5,0.5]\times {1}={(k,1)\,:\,k\in [-0.5,0.5]}.
$$

This represents a horizontal line segment from the point $(-0.5,1)$ to the point $(0.5,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/6c6aafd9ea78868e953340eaab3862491d275972d690e2ceb27c213dadbcaea6.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}=[-i,i]\times {2i}={(k,2i)\,:\,k\in [-i,i]}
$$

is the horizontal line segment from the point $(-i,2i)$ to the point $(i,2i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/02c8f93a25d7b510d3e238e6d4a974d6ccc2e83f3ac01fe92ce4535fbb4dce48.png)

As $i$ runs over $I,$ these line segments sweep the following triangle that represents the union ${⋃}_{i\in I}{X}_{i}:$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3b3cefa03d71d99e4b7f3b6852ed36512d2a841a37c558034eac5c4b6870799c.png)

q-184505:
Recall that the union of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *at least one* set:

$$
{⋃}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for at least one}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=0.5,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{0.5}={0.5}\times [0,0.125]={(0.5,k)\,:\,k\in [0,0.125]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(0.5,0)$ to the point $(0.5,0.125)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/3a1bb7a7c54718e39df80092243a119ec8b5a6e77ec4f9d58ffb074e50191d04.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,{i}^{3}]={(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,{i}^{3}]}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,{i}^{3}).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/472b6456019a5c89e585f80aa4a0dfd44f3b87c0624c10ea7b52f32e958a8c4e.png)

q-172690:
Recall that the intersection of a family of indexed sets consists of those elements that belong to *all* the sets:

$$
{⋂}_{i\in I}{A}_{i}={x\,:\,x\in {A}_{k}\,\,\text{for all}\,\,k\in I}
$$

Let's now write down one of our indexed sets. For example, if $i=1,$ we have 

$$
{X}_{1}={1}\times [0,1]={(1,k)\,:\,k\in [0,1]}.
$$

This represents a vertical line segment from the point $(1,0)$ to the point $(1,1)$ in the coordinate plane, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/71dd97607df48caf579c2e476520507ede035f65c336064f022cd900b6c120fc.png)

In general,

$$
{X}_{i}={i}\times [0,i]={(i,k)\,:\,k\in [0,i]}
$$

is the vertical line segment from the point $(i,0)$ to the point $(i,i).$ 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14072804/assets/4b87c830620f54e5b3a3bb7923be971b4d9d4abb98cfb3dcdc8387f376a0b452.png)

There are no points that lie in all sets. Therefore, the intersection of the indexed sets is $∅,$ the empty set.

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A} & =\overset{―}{[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3-2\text{i} & 4\text{i} \\ -1-3\text{i} & 5 & 3-5\text{i} \\ 2+\text{i} & -5-\text{i} & -3+3\text{i}\end{aligned}]} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{-4} & \overset{―}{3-2\text{i}} & \overset{―}{4\text{i}} \\ \overset{―}{-1-3\text{i}} & \overset{―}{5} & \overset{―}{3-5\text{i}} \\ \overset{―}{2+\text{i}} & \overset{―}{-5-\text{i}} & \overset{―}{-3+3\text{i}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4 & 3+2\text{i} & -4\text{i} \\ -1+3\text{i} & 5 & 3+5\text{i} \\ 2-\text{i} & -5+\text{i} & -3-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, ${b}_{31}+{b}_{32}=(2-\text{i})+(-5+\text{i})=-3.$

q-76057:
Taking the complex conjugate of each entry, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{A} & =\overset{―}{[\begin{aligned}9-7\text{i} & -2\text{i} & 6-\text{i} \\ -7 & 5-\text{i} & \text{i} \\ 6 & -\text{i} & 0\end{aligned}]} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{9-7\text{i}} & \overset{―}{-2\text{i}} & \overset{―}{6-\text{i}} \\ \overset{―}{-7} & \overset{―}{5-\text{i}} & \overset{―}{\text{i}} \\ \overset{―}{6} & \overset{―}{-\text{i}} & \overset{―}{0}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}9+7\text{i} & 2\text{i} & 6+\text{i} \\ -7 & 5+\text{i} & -\text{i} \\ 6 & \text{i} & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-76203:
For the given matrix $A,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} & 5\text{i} \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0-3\text{i} & 0+5\text{i} \\ -4+0\text{i} & 5+0\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}0 & 0 \\ -4 & 5\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(A)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-3 & 5 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(A)}.\end{aligned}
$$

So we have $a=0,c=-4,f=5$ and $h=0.$ Therefore,

$$
ah-cf=0\cdot 0-(-4)\cdot 5=20.
$$

q-76204:
For the given matrix $A,$ we have that

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} & 7-6\text{i} \\ -\text{i} & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} & 7-6\text{i} \\ 0-\text{i} & 4+0\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & ={{[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(A)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}2 & -6 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(A)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\text{Re}(A)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 7 \\ 0 & 4\end{aligned}].$

q-76217:
Multiplying the matrices using the usual method, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}2-3\text{i} & \text{i} \\ 3 & -1-\text{i}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2\text{i} & 5 \\ 1-4\text{i} & 2+\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(2-3\text{i})\cdot 2\text{i}+\text{i}\cdot (1-4\text{i}) & (2-3\text{i})\cdot 5+\text{i}\cdot (2+\text{i}) \\ 3\cdot 2\text{i}+(-1-\text{i})(1-4\text{i}) & 3\cdot 5+(-1-\text{i})(2+\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(4\text{i}+6)+(\text{i}+4) & (10-15\text{i})+(2\text{i}-1) \\ 6\text{i}+(-5+3\text{i}) & 15+(-1-3\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10+5\text{i} & 9-13\text{i} \\ -5+9\text{i} & 14-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-140329:
Multiplying the matrix by the vector using the usual method, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =[\begin{aligned}-3+5\text{i} & 4-3\text{i} \\ -4\text{i} & 5-5\text{i}\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3\text{i} \\ 4-5\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(-3+5\text{i})(-3\text{i})+(4-3\text{i})(4-5\text{i}) \\ (-4\text{i})(-3\text{i})+(5-5\text{i})(4-5\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}(15+9\text{i})+(1-32\text{i}) \\ (-12)+(-5-45\text{i})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}16-23\text{i} \\ -17-45\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

q-140381:
Let's apply the row operations to $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} & -2-4\text{i} \\ 3-2\text{i} & \text{i}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{1} & :=\frac{1}{1+2\text{i}}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 3-2\text{i} & \text{i}\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(2\text{i}-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 6-3\text{i}\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the result is

$$
[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 6-3\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

q-35965:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $Q$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=q+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $q$ is the position vector of $Q.$

In our case, the position vector of the point $Q$ is $q=⟨-3,3,3⟩.$

Using the formula for the vector equation of a line, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}r=⟨-3,3,3⟩+t⟨\frac{\sqrt{2}}{3},-5,3⟩,\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-69773:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $H$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=h+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $h$ is the position vector of $H.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $H(5,7,2)$ and $S(3,4,5),$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{HS} \\  & =⟨3,4,5⟩-⟨5,7,2⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,-3,3⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}5 \\ 7 \\ 2\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

q-126752:
The vector equation of the straight line passing through $P$ and parallel to $v$ is given by

$$
r=p+tv,
$$

where $t\in (-\infty ,\infty )$ and $p$ is the position vector of $P.$ 

We can find a direction vector by computing the displacement vector between the given points $P(0,1,3)$ and $Q(3,-4,-2)$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\overset{\to }{PQ} \\  & =⟨3,-4,-2⟩-⟨0,1,3⟩ \\  & =⟨3,-5,-5⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector equation of the line is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]+t[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -5 \\ -5\end{aligned}],\,t\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$
